findings.explanation: Since April 2023 every new S3 bucket is created with Object Ownership = BucketOwnerEnforced, which disables ACLs outright. Applying an aws_s3_bucket_acl to such a bucket fails with AccessControlListNotSupported. The module creates no aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls resource, so the bucket takes that default and this resource can never apply. No rule catches it because the failure lives in the absence of a third resource plus a provider-side default that changed date, not in any attribute of either resource present. The principle is a best-fit: this is apply-time correctness, not a security gap.
findings.remediation: Add an aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls with object_ownership = "BucketOwnerPreferred" and make the ACL depend on it, or drop aws_s3_bucket_acl entirely — BucketOwnerEnforced already gives the private-by-default behaviour acl = "private" was asking for, and the public access block covers the rest.
findings.title: aws_s3_bucket_acl cannot apply: bucket has no ownership controls and defaults to BucketOwnerEnforced

findings.explanation: var.is_organization_trail is a supported input, but an organization trail writes to <prefix>/AWSLogs/<org-id>/<account-id>/CloudTrail/... while the AWSCloudTrailWrite statement only permits arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/<prefix>/AWSLogs/<account-id>/*. Turning the flag on therefore has CloudTrail rejected at the bucket-policy validation, or silently unable to deliver. The Glue table's storage_descriptor.location hardcodes the same non-org path, so Athena would query an empty prefix even if delivery worked. A rule cannot see this: it requires knowing that one variable's value changes the S3 key layout that a different resource's JSON string encodes.
findings.remediation: Derive the AWSLogs path owner from a new var.organization_id (o-xxxxxxxxxx, default null) rather than data.aws_organizations_organization, which errors outright for any account not in an organization and would break every consumer without one. Grant both the account path and the org path in the bucket policy, as AWS's reference org-trail policy does, and guard the combination with a variable validation so is_organization_trail = true without an organization_id fails at plan time rather than mid-apply.
findings.title: Setting is_organization_trail breaks log delivery: bucket policy and Glue table hardcode the non-org S3 path

findings.explanation: The trust policy allows cloudtrail.amazonaws.com to assume the role with no aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceArn condition. A service principal is not scoped to your account: any account's CloudTrail can ask the service to assume a role that trusts it, which is the confused-deputy pattern AWS documents for every service-principal trust. The attached policy is tight (logs:CreateLogStream / logs:PutLogEvents on one log group), so blast radius is log injection into your CloudWatch group rather than data theft — but the missing condition is the control AWS explicitly prescribes. HLD_AWS_276 only rejects wildcard principals, so a named service principal passes it.
findings.remediation: Add a Condition to the assume_role_policy statement: "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:SourceAccount": "<account-id>"}} using data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id, and ideally aws:SourceArn scoped to the trail ARN.
findings.title: CloudTrail service trust policy has no aws:SourceAccount condition (cross-account confused deputy)

findings.explanation: Both the AWSCloudTrailAclCheck and AWSCloudTrailWrite statements grant cloudtrail.amazonaws.com with no aws:SourceArn condition. The write statement is largely self-limiting because its Resource pins the account ID into the key path, but AWSCloudTrailAclCheck grants s3:GetBucketAcl on the bucket to any account's CloudTrail, letting an outsider who guesses the bucket name (trails-<account-id>, entirely predictable) confirm it exists. AWS's own reference policy carries aws:SourceArn on both statements for this reason.
findings.remediation: Add "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudtrail:<region>:<account>:trail/<name>"}} to both statements, building the ARN from data sources and var.trail["name"] rather than referencing aws_cloudtrail.account.arn, which would invert the dependency order.
findings.title: S3 bucket policy grants CloudTrail service principal without aws:SourceArn
aws_cloudtrail does not wait for its S3 bucket policy or CloudWatch Logs role policy, so first apply can race
findings.explanation: The trail references aws_s3_bucket.trails.id and aws_iam_role.cloudtrail.arn, never the bucket policy or the role policy, so Terraform is free to create the trail before either exists. CreateTrail validates the bucket policy up front and fails with InsufficientS3BucketPolicyException when it is not yet in place; the logs role can fail the same way with InvalidCloudWatchLogsRoleArnException. The existing depends_on already acknowledges this exact ordering problem for the SNS topic policy but stops there, and no rule can see it because it is an absence of a dependency edge between three resources. The principle is a best fit: this is apply-time correctness, not a security gap.
findings.remediation: Extend depends_on to also list aws_s3_bucket_policy.trails and aws_iam_role_policy.cloudtrail.

findings.title: KMS key policy does not let CloudTrail publish to the key-encrypted SNS notification topic
findings.explanation: aws_sns_topic.cloudtrail is encrypted with this CMK, so cloudtrail.amazonaws.com needs kms:GenerateDataKey* and kms:Decrypt on it to publish. The only CloudTrail GenerateDataKey* grant is conditioned on kms:EncryptionContext:aws:cloudtrail:arn, but SNS uses the aws:sns:topicArn context, so it does not match, and no kms:Decrypt is granted to the service principal at all. The trail applies cleanly while delivery notifications are dropped with a KMS access error, which only shows up at runtime. Confidence is medium because it rests on the SNS encryption-context behaviour rather than anything in the code.
findings.remediation: Add a key policy statement allowing cloudtrail.amazonaws.com kms:GenerateDataKey* and kms:Decrypt, scoped with aws:SourceArn equal to the trail ARN, or stop encrypting the notification topic with this key.

suggested_policies.rationale: An aws_s3_bucket_acl with no aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls in the same configuration is a guaranteed apply failure on any bucket created after April 2023, when BucketOwnerEnforced became the default and ACLs stopped being accepted. It is a pure companion-resource condition on a specific resource type, fires correctly on any Terraform using aws_s3_bucket_acl, and neither HLD_AWS_290 nor HLD_AWS_296 (the only two policies covering aws_s3_bucket_acl) touches ownership controls.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_AWS_315
name: S3 bucket ACLs require explicit ownership controls
principle: reliability
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  Since April 2023 new S3 buckets default to Object Ownership =
  BucketOwnerEnforced, which disables ACLs entirely. Applying an
  aws_s3_bucket_acl to such a bucket fails with AccessControlListNotSupported.
  An aws_s3_bucket_acl is therefore only applyable when an
  aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls resource explicitly sets
  BucketOwnerPreferred or ObjectWriter first.
remediation: |
  Either drop the ACL — BucketOwnerEnforced already denies public access, and
  an aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block covers the rest — or declare the
  ownership controls the ACL depends on:

    resource "aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls" "example" {
      bucket = aws_s3_bucket.example.id
      rule {
        object_ownership = "BucketOwnerPreferred"
      }
    }

    resource "aws_s3_bucket_acl" "example" {
      bucket     = aws_s3_bucket.example.id
      acl        = "private"
      depends_on = [aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls.example]
    }
compliance:
  checkov: CKV2_AWS_65
resources:
  aws_s3_bucket_acl:
    requires_companion:
      type: aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls
      linked_via:
        from: bucket
        to: bucket

suggested_policies.rationale: An IAM trust policy naming an AWS service principal with no aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceArn condition is the documented confused-deputy shape, and it is statically decidable from the assume_role_policy JSON alone: a Statement whose Principal.Service is set but which carries no Condition constraining the calling account. HLD_AWS_276 covers only wildcard principals, so every named service principal passes today. Applies to any provider resource using assume_role_policy.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_AWS_316
name: Service-principal trust policies must be scoped by source account or ARN
principle: identity-and-access
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  An AWS service principal such as cloudtrail.amazonaws.com is not scoped to
  your account. Any customer's resource in that service can ask the service to
  assume a role that trusts it, so a trust policy naming a service principal
  without an aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceArn condition can be exercised on
  behalf of a resource you do not own — the confused-deputy pattern AWS
  documents for every service-to-service trust.
remediation: |
  Constrain the trust statement to your own account or the specific resource:

    assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
      Version = "2012-10-17"
      Statement = [{
        Effect    = "Allow"
        Principal = { Service = "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com" }
        Action    = "sts:AssumeRole"
        Condition = {
          StringEquals = {
            "aws:SourceAccount" = data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id
          }
        }
      }]
    })
resources:
  aws_iam_role:
    path: assume_role_policy
    json_decode: true
    sub_path: Statement
    not_any:
      all:
        - path: Principal.Service
          not_null: true
        - path: Condition
          absent: true

suggested_policies.rationale: An aws_cloudtrail whose configuration also declares an aws_s3_bucket_policy for the same bucket must depend on that policy, because CreateTrail validates the bucket policy and nothing in the resource references it. It applies to any Terraform using aws_cloudtrail, and coverage_by_type for aws_cloudtrail (HLD_AWS_001/005/014/079/080/094/161/194/311/379) has no policy on apply ordering.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: LOCAL_AWS_001
name: CloudTrail trails must depend on their S3 bucket policy
principle: reliability
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  CreateTrail validates the destination bucket policy before it succeeds. The
  trail references only the bucket, never the policy, so without an explicit
  depends_on Terraform can create the trail first and fail with
  InsufficientS3BucketPolicyException.
message: |
  aws_cloudtrail does not depend_on the aws_s3_bucket_policy of its bucket.
remediation: |
  Add the bucket policy to the trail:
    depends_on = [aws_s3_bucket_policy.trails]
resources:
  aws_cloudtrail:
    requires_companion:
      type: aws_s3_bucket_policy
      via: bucket
